case.title: Analytics Manager work-sample: Trust & Safety enforcement metrics, an experiment readout, and an opportunity-sizing ask
case.brief: You are stepping in as Analytics Manager for a Trust & Safety / integrity analytics team that measures enforcement on a large global platform. You own the topline enforcement KPI that leadership watches weekly, you manage a small team of analysts, and Product and Engineering treat you as the quantitative partner on what to build and what it's worth. This case hands you three live situations a manager in this seat faces in the same week: a topline number you're not sure you trust, a junior analyst's experiment readout sitting in your queue for sign-off, and a vague opportunity-sizing request from a Product partner. None of these is a typing test — assume any SQL, Python, or R you produce can be generated for you in seconds, so what's being assessed is your judgment: what you read before you trust it, how you verify a 'significant' result, how you size an under-specified ask, and how you coach versus do-it-yourself. NOTE ON MATERIALS: the role's own context (SQL/stats/BI/A-B/enforcement) fits this exercise, but no real dashboard or warehouse was supplied with the JD, so the starting materials below are synthetic but representative of a Meta-style internal analytics environment (Hive/Presto/Daiquery-class warehouse, weekly KPI dashboards, experiment platform). Treat them as your real inbox. Hard cap: ~2 hours — favor depth and defensible judgment over volume; you are not expected to write production pipelines.
case.repoSeed: A small bundle representing your first week in the seat: (1) `enforcement_kpi_dashboard.sql` — the Presto query that feeds the weekly leadership dashboard, including an `enforcement_coverage_rate` CTE and an `action_rate` CTE; it joins `integrity.content_reviews` to `integrity.actions_daily` and the coverage rate's denominator is built from reviewed items only. (2) `experiment_readout.md` (with an attached `readout.ipynb` sketch) — a junior analyst's analysis of a new enforcement classifier rollout, reporting a '+6.2% precision lift, p=0.03, ship it' against control, computed with a two-sample t-test on a per-decision basis and segmented loosely across three regions. (3) `warehouse_tables.md` — a data dictionary for the relevant tables: `integrity.actions_daily`, `integrity.content_reviews`, `integrity.appeals`, `experiments.assignment_log` (unit, region, bucket, day), and `partner.experience_survey`. (4) `opportunity_request.txt` — a two-line message from a Product partner: 'How big is the opportunity if we improve enforcement on marketplace listings next half? Need a number for planning by Friday.' (5) `team_snapshot.md` — one paragraph each on four analysts (two early-career, one senior IC, one ready-for-lead), naming each person's current growth edge.
tasks: Audit the topline enforcement KPI. Read `enforcement_kpi_dashboard.sql` before changing anything and decide whether the weekly `enforcement_coverage_rate` number leadership sees is trustworthy. State precisely what the metric currently measures versus what it's presented as measuring, quantify (with assumptions if needed) how far off it could be, recommend a fix to the definition, and decide what you tell leadership this week — corrected number now, caveated trend, or wait. Don't just regenerate a cleaner query; diagnose the existing one.

Sign off — or don't — on `experiment_readout.md` as the analyst's manager. Determine whether the claimed lift is real enough to ship a classifier change that affects enforcement decisions on real partners. Then write the technical-mentorship feedback you would actually send this analyst: specific, developmental, calibrated to an early-career level, separating the method issue from the ship decision. Conclude with your call: ship, hold, or limited rollout, and why.

Respond to the Product partner's opportunity-sizing request in `opportunity_request.txt`. First write the clarifying questions you'd send back and why each one changes the answer. Then, without waiting for replies, produce a defensible first-cut size with your assumptions, your chosen impact metric, and the method stated explicitly, and recommend whether this opportunity clears the bar to prioritize against other work. A confident single number with no stated assumptions is a fail condition here.

Keep a short DECISIONS log (normal practice, not a separate exercise) covering Tasks 1–3: for every call you made where the brief was open — the metric definition you settled on, what you'd ship/hold, the impact metric you sized against, how directive you chose to be with the analyst — record what you chose, the alternative you rejected and why, and the one question you'd put to the team or partner before committing for real.

coverProbes.where: Task 1 — the `enforcement_coverage_rate` CTE in `enforcement_kpi_dashboard.sql`, whose denominator is built from reviewed items only
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate reads the existing SQL and recognizes the coverage rate is survivorship-biased — computed over already-reviewed content, so it overstates true coverage and the healthy weekly trend is partly an artifact of the denominator. A naive one-shot response regenerates a tidy fresh query that reproduces the same reviewed-only denominator (or ignores the definition entirely) and reports the headline number as sound.
decisionSpace: Preserve the legacy definition but annotate it with an explicit caveat, prioritizing continuity of the historical trend leadership already anchors on
Redefine the metric over the true eligible population and re-baseline, accepting a break in historical comparability and an awkward conversation about why the number moved
Report both the legacy and corrected figures side by side this week and flag the gap explicitly so leadership sees the bias rather than a silent restatement

coverProbes.where: Task 2 — the '+6.2% precision lift, p=0.03' significance claim in `experiment_readout.md`, plus the assignment counts in `experiments.assignment_log`
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate won't take p=0.03 at face value: precision is a ratio metric so a naive per-decision two-sample t-test understates variance (delta method / clustered SE needed), and a quick check of `assignment_log` bucket counts can surface a sample-ratio mismatch or a region-level confound (Simpson's paradox) that invalidates the pooled result. A naive response accepts the reported p-value and approves shipping.
decisionSpace: Hold and re-run with corrected variance and an SRM/segment check before any rollout — correctness over speed
Ship behind a holdback/guardrail given the cost of delay, with live monitoring and a pre-committed rollback trigger
Roll out only to the region where the effect is robust and re-test the segments where the signal is confounded

coverProbes.where: Task 3 — the two-line opportunity-sizing ask in `opportunity_request.txt` with no target metric, baseline, or segment defined
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate names the missing pieces (which harm/metric, what baseline, which listing segment, over what horizon) and frames assumptions before computing, treating the number as a function of stated choices. A naive response emits one confident figure with no method or assumptions, hiding the leverage points that actually determine the answer.
decisionSpace: Size by prevalence / harm reduction — the platform-impact framing of 'better enforcement'
Size by reviewer-cost or operational efficiency saved — the cost framing
Size by partner-experience proxy (false-positive and appeal reduction) — the trust/experience framing

coverProbes.where: Tasks 2 & 4 — how directive versus developmental the mentorship feedback is, and what you choose to own versus escalate
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate calibrates the feedback to an early-career analyst and keeps the teachable method-error distinct from the time-sensitive ship decision, neither doing the analysis for them nor rubber-stamping. A naive response either silently rewrites the readout (robbing the development moment) or only validates the conclusion without surfacing the statistical flaw.
decisionSpace: Directive fix now because the correctness risk is urgent, with the coaching conversation deferred to a 1:1
Developmental — guide the analyst to find the flaw themselves via pointed questions, accepting a slower turnaround
Pair on it and co-own the corrected readout, trading some scalability for a faster, shared-learning outcome
